PhyRubric: Rubric-Grounded Diagnostic Evaluation of Physical Commonsense in Text-to-Video Generation

Huiyi Chen    Weitai Kang    Shicheng Fan    Xinshuo Wang Affiliation: Zhixiang Shen    Yan Yan    Philip S. Yu    Baoxin Li Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, University of Illinois Chicago Affiliation: {hchen270, wkang126, sfan25, xwang921, zshen33, yyan55, psyu, baoxinli}@uic.edu Affiliation: https://github.com/chenyil6/phyRubric
Abstract

As text-to-video (T2V) models are increasingly positioned as world simulators, it is essential to evaluate whether their videos conform to physical commonsense. However, existing benchmarks rely on annotators who rate each video with a single score based on intuition, yielding ratings that are subjective and do not tell which physical principle is violated. We introduce PhyRubric, a rubric-grounded diagnostic framework for evaluating physical commonsense in T2V generation. For each caption, PhyRubric constructs a caption-specific rubric before any video is seen, decomposing the caption into semantic and physical items, and derives scores from item-level verdicts grounded in timestamped evidence. We instantiate this framework as PhyRubric-Bench, which spans 34 categories across five physical domains, and scale it up to PhyRubric-Train with 3,788 videos, on which we fine-tune the open-source PhyRubric-Judge. Empirical results across ten T2V models show that physical commonsense remains far from solved, and that PhyRubric-Judge correlates more closely with human judgments than existing open-source judges while matching the frontier proprietary Gemini 4 Argon. Further analysis provides actionable insights for T2V models.

1 Introduction

Text-to-video (T2V) generation has advanced rapidly, and recent T2V models [59, 62, 1, 14, 67, 57, 45] can now render complex scenes from text prompts. As these models are increasingly positioned as world simulators [68, 33, 1], a basic requirement is that their videos conform to physical commonsense, the shared expectations about the physical world that everyone acquires from everyday experience, without any textbook physics [37, 55]. A reliable and comprehensive evaluation of this ability is therefore essential for tracking progress and guiding model development.

Existing benchmarks for physical commonsense have made notable progress [7, 8, 47, 19], but they share two limitations (Fig. 1). First, the ratings are subjective. Annotators rate each video and its caption with a single score on a discrete scale, but no rule defines how physical violations map to scores. Each rater thus applies an intuitive mapping, weighing the severity of violations by personal standards, so the same video may receive different scores. This inconsistency introduces noise into both benchmark results and the automatic evaluators trained on these ratings. Second, the ratings are uninterpretable. A discrete scale is easier to rate than a continuous one, since fractional scores would be harder to assign and more scattered. However, a single score reflects only how implausible a video is overall, not which physical principle is violated. Evaluations can thus only rank models and categories, yielding coarse findings that offer little guidance for improvement.

To address these limitations, we introduce PhyRubric, a rubric-grounded diagnostic framework for evaluating physical commonsense in T2V generation (Fig. 2). For each caption, PhyRubric constructs a caption-specific rubric before any video is seen, and reuses it for every video generated from that caption. The rubric decomposes the caption into verifiable items of two types: semantic items list the visible facts the caption requires, while physical items specify which visible events count as violations and are each assigned a severity level inspired by the order in which infants acquire physical knowledge [55, 6, 41]. Given a video, each item receives a verdict grounded in timestamped evidence, and scores are derived deterministically from these verdicts rather than rated directly. Every score thus comes with a diagnosis of which expectation failed and why.

We instantiate this framework as PhyRubric-Bench. Unlike prior benchmarks dominated by mechanics (Suppl. Tab. 4), it spans 34 categories across five physical domains: mechanics, optics, heat, electricity, and acoustics11 1 Since generated videos are silent, the acoustics domain covers only the visible consequences of sound, such as water rippling beside a speaker.. Every caption describes a complete causal event and states its outcome explicitly, so that semantic adherence requires rendering the cause, the action, and its physical consequence, e.g., “the key switch is turned, and the lamp lights” rather than “the key switch is turned.”

Beyond PhyRubric-Bench, we scale up to PhyRubric-Train, 947 captions that share the taxonomy of the benchmark but no scenes, each paired with its own rubric. Here the rubric plays a different role: rather than defining the evaluation as in PhyRubric-Bench, it guides an agentic annotator, telling it which expectations to check and where to look, yielding 3,788 labeled videos from four T2V models with 45.9K rubric-item verdicts. On these labels, we train PhyRubric-Judge, an open-source VLM that needs no rubric at inference. Given only a caption and a video, it predicts semantic adherence and physical commonsense scores together with a diagnosis of which physical expectation is violated and why.

We evaluate ten T2V models on PhyRubric-Bench and find that basic physical commonsense remains far from solved: even the strongest model, Seedance 2.5, produces videos that are both faithful to the caption and physically plausible in fewer than half of cases. Moreover, PhyRubric-Judge correlates more closely with human judgments than the judges released with existing benchmarks, generalizes well to unseen generators and domains, and provides a diagnosis that locates each violation.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We propose PhyRubric, a rubric-grounded framework that constructs a caption-specific rubric before any video is seen and derives every score from evidence-grounded item verdicts, so that each score comes with a diagnosis.

  • •

    We construct PhyRubric-Bench, spanning 34 categories across five physical domains with human-verified rubrics and labels, and PhyRubric-Train, labeled by a rubric-guided agentic annotator, on which we train the open-source PhyRubric-Judge that generalizes to unseen generators and domains.

  • •

    Rather than proposing a definitive standard, we show that our rubric-grounded evaluation serves as an analysis tool that yields deeper insights: semantic adherence is the main bottleneck, physical errors are all-or-nothing, and models often avoid physical errors by not depicting the event at all, a shortcut that prior protocols reward.

2 Related Work

2.1 Physical Commonsense Benchmarks for Text-to-Video Generation

The rapid advancement of text-to-video (T2V) generation has motivated a range of benchmarks for its assessment [30, 66, 31, 43, 60, 56, 44, 39]. Moving beyond general visual quality, a growing line of work focuses on physical commonsense in T2V generation [7, 8, 47, 19, 20, 53, 36], while other works study physical understanding in settings where models are conditioned on observed frames and predict how the scene evolves [48, 33, 40]. However, most of these physical commonsense benchmarks are dominated by mechanics [7, 8, 20], and some include prompts that require specialized knowledge beyond everyday experience [47, 19, 20, 36]. In contrast, PhyRubric-Bench spans five physical domains with prompts grounded in physical commonsense, and pairs each prompt with a caption-specific rubric that enables diagnostic evaluation.

2.2 VLM-as-a-Judge for Physical Commonsense

Existing evaluation of video generation mainly follows two paradigms: standard metrics such as FVD [58], SSIM [61], and CLIP score [27], and VLM-based evaluation [12, 52, 23] such as VideoScore [26]. As standard metrics cannot capture physical plausibility, physical commonsense evaluation mainly adopts the latter, employing VLMs as dedicated judges. On the open-source side, judges such as VideoCon-Physics [7] and VideoPhy-2-AutoEval [8] are fine-tuned on the human annotations of their corresponding datasets. On the proprietary side, recent works prompt commercial models such as GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro, and GPT-5.5 as judges [47, 19, 53, 51]. Nevertheless, most of these judges output a holistic score rather than a detailed diagnosis, failing to reveal what goes wrong and why.

2.3 Rubric-Based Evaluation

A rubric is an explicit set of criteria that decomposes a holistic quality judgment into verifiable items, making the assessment transparent, consistent, and interpretable [32, 13]. Recently, rubrics have been widely adopted for fine-grained evaluation of large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models [34, 38], and increasingly tailor the criteria to each individual query rather than applying a generic rubric to all samples [35, 16, 4]. In text-to-image generation, a related line of work decomposes prompts into fine-grained questions to assess text-image alignment [29, 15]. However, rubric-based evaluation remains underexplored for physical commonsense in video generation. In this work, rubrics play two roles: they serve as the evaluation criteria of PhyRubric-Bench, and they guide an agentic annotator to label training data for PhyRubric-Judge.

3 PhyRubric

As illustrated in Fig. 2, PhyRubric fixes a rubric for each caption before any video is seen and shares it across all videos from that caption. This keeps the criteria identical across videos, so that scores from different generators are directly comparable and cannot be swayed by what a particular video happens to show. Moreover, a rubric reviewed by humans once can be reused for any number of videos, including those from future generators.

3.1 Caption-Specific Rubric Formulation

We evaluate generated videos along the two dimensions introduced by VideoPhy-2 [8], semantic adherence (SA) and physical commonsense (PC), each on a 1–5 scale. Unlike prior benchmarks, where annotators assign a holistic score to each dimension, we pair every caption with a rubric that specifies what a video must satisfy to be faithful and physically plausible for that caption. The rubric consists of two groups of items, one for SA and one for PC, and each score is derived from item-level verdicts rather than rated directly. A simplified rubric example is shown in Fig. 3.

Semantic Adherence (SA). SA measures whether the video shows what the caption describes. Its rubric items are the visible facts the caption requires, in two tiers:

  • •

    Primary: the main objects and each event in the caption.

  • •

    Secondary: the remaining facts, including stated qualifiers (e.g., once, slowly, wooden), initial states implied by the caption, and the order of events.

Physical Commonsense (PC). This metric evaluates whether the events shown in the video follow physical commonsense. We define four severity levels for physical violations, inspired by the order in which infants acquire physical knowledge in developmental psychology [55, 6, 41]:

  • •

    Fatal: the scene is impossible as a whole, violating core object principles such as permanence, solidity, or continuity (e.g., objects passing through each other, or appearing or vanishing without cause).

  • •

    Core: the central interaction described by the caption does not happen or happens incorrectly (e.g., in reverse or through a broken mechanism).

  • •

    Major: a clear violation outside the central interaction, such as a missing secondary consequence (e.g., the lamp lights but the desk beneath it stays dark).

  • •

    Minor: a visual flaw that leaves the event intact, such as color or texture drift of untouched objects.

Each PC item is assigned one of these severity levels and one of ten violation types (e.g., permanence, solidity, causeless motion, process direction). Following the same developmental order, the ten types are grouped into L1 core object principles, L2 everyday dynamics, and L3 attribute experience (Suppl. Tab. 6). Each PC item is then judged by a pair of verifiable statements:

  • •

    Expect: what a physically correct video should show, specifying the moment, region, or event to inspect.

  • •

    Fail: the concrete visible signs that count as a violation, and the item fails only if one of these signs is observed.

Verdicts. An SA item is judged pass or fail. A PC item has a third verdict, not shown, which applies when the moment, region, or event specified by its Expect statement never appears in the video. Otherwise, the item fails if any sign in its Fail statement is observed, and passes if not. Note that not shown means the situation is absent, not that the expected behavior failed to occur. For example, for the caption “The key switch on the base of a desk lamp is turned, and the lamp lights” (Fig. 3), if the key is never turned in the video, P2 is not shown rather than failed, since the missing action is already penalized by the SA item S2. Since a fail can only be triggered by a listed sign, every negative verdict is grounded in a specific observation rather than an overall impression, and carries the severity and violation type of its item. Consistent with the nature of commonsense, PC items judge only the direction and order of change rather than its rate or extent, and never penalize a cause for being out of view (e.g., a heat source or power supply).

Scoring Rules. Both scores lie on a 1–5 scale and are derived from the verdicts by fixed rules. For SA, a video judged entirely unrelated to the caption scores 1. Otherwise, it scores 5 if all items pass, 4 if only secondary items fail, 3 if exactly one primary item fails, and 2 if two or more primary items fail. For PC, let FF be the set of failed items. A video with F=∅F=\emptyset scores 5; otherwise,

PC=max⁡(1,mini∈F⁡c⁡(si)−max⁡(0,h−1)),\mathrm{PC}=\max\big(1,\;\min_{i\in F}c(s_{i})-\max(0,\,h-1)\big), (1)

where sis_{i} is the severity of item ii, c⁡(⋅)c(\cdot) maps fatal, core, major, and minor to caps of 1, 2, 3, and 4, and hh is the number of failed items of major severity or above. In words, the most severe failure sets the cap, and each additional failure of major severity or above lowers the score by one. Each rubric is checked to contain at least two primary and one secondary SA items and at least one PC item of every severity, so that every score from 1 to 5 is attainable.

3.2 PhyRubric-Bench

Suppl. Tab. 4 compares PhyRubric-Bench with prior benchmarks, which are dominated by mechanics. PhyRubric-Bench covers all five physical domains with 34 categories (Fig. 4), and every caption tests only physical commonsense and is paired with a human-verified rubric.

Caption and rubric generation. Captions are drafted by Claude Fable 5.1 [2] and GPT-5.6 Sol [49] and refined by human reviewers until each describes a single causal event that is visible within about five seconds and has an explicitly stated outcome. Stating the outcome serves two purposes. (1) Fixed expectations: what should happen is determined before any video is seen, so the rubric can specify the expected events and violations rather than guess among plausible outcomes. (2) Diagnostic failures: if a model is told what should happen yet fails to render it, the failure reflects missing physical knowledge rather than creative freedom.

In addition, captions include a person only when the human body itself is part of the physics, since current generators often produce distorted human bodies [66, 65, 46]. Each phenomenon is instantiated in three to five distinct scenes for diversity, yielding 1,192 captions, which are split into 245 for PhyRubric-Bench and 947 for PhyRubric-Train (Sec. 3.3) with no scene shared between the two. Each caption is then paired with a rubric, drafted by an LLM prompted with example rubrics from the same domain, checked automatically for format and score reachability, and revised by human reviewers until approved.

Video generation and annotation. For evaluation, the 245 benchmark captions are rendered by ten text-to-video models, six of which are unseen during judge training, yielding 2,433 videos22 2 The remaining 17 of the 10×24510\times 245 videos were not produced because the generators’ built-in safety filters declined the captions.. Each video is first pre-annotated item by item by our agentic annotator (Sec. 3.3), and human annotators then verify every verdict against the video to obtain the ground truth. Since the rubric already specifies what counts as a violation, annotators only need to check whether the listed signs appear, rather than judging physical plausibility themselves. More construction details and statistics are given in Suppl. Sec. A.2.

3.3 PhyRubric-Train and PhyRubric-Judge

Training data annotation. Human verification does not scale to thousands of videos, so we label the training set with the same agentic annotator used to pre-annotate PhyRubric-Bench, built on Claude Sonnet 5.5 [3]. Instead of a fixed set of frames, the annotator first scans a timestamped overview of the clip and then zooms in at full frame rate where and when it needs to, until each rubric item can be decided from frames that clearly show the relevant event. This matters because physical violations often involve small objects or brief moments that uniform sampling misses. For every item, it returns a verdict with timestamped evidence, and the scores follow from the verdicts by the rules in Sec. 3.1. Applied to the 947 training captions, each rendered by four generators, it yields PhyRubric-Train with 3,788 videos and 45.9K item-level verdicts. Suppl. Sec. A.4 details its protocol and reliability.

Judge. The agentic annotator produces reliable labels but is impractical as a general-purpose evaluator: it relies on a proprietary model, makes repeated tool calls per video, and needs a rubric for every new caption. We therefore train PhyRubric-Judge, an open-source VLM, on PhyRubric-Train. Starting from Qwen3-VL-8B [5], we explore configurations that vary the rubric input, the output format, and the training objective (SFT or GRPO [54]). Our default judge takes only the caption and uniformly sampled frames, so that it applies to any new caption and receives the same input as existing judges. It outputs the SA score, whether PC is assessable, the PC score, and a diagnosis. The training targets come from PhyRubric-Train, with the diagnosis assembled from the item-level evidence: a summary of what the video shows, the missing caption facts, and each physical violation with its evidence. The judge thus learns not only what score to give but why (Suppl. Sec. C.3).

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

Video Generative Models. PhyRubric-Bench is rendered by ten video generators. Four of them are open-source T2V models that also render PhyRubric-Train: CogVideoX1.5-5B [64], HunyuanVideo-1.5-8B [62], LTX-Video-2B [22], and Wan2.2-T2V-A14B [59]. The other six are unseen during training and measure how well a judge generalizes to new generators: Wan2.2-TI2V-5B [59], LTX-2.3-22B [21], Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B and Cosmos-Predict2.5-14B [1], and the proprietary Seedance 2.5 [11] and Veo 3.1 [17]. All videos are five to six seconds long.

Evaluation Metrics. Each video is rated on a 1–5 scale for SA and PC. We report the mean SA over all videos and the mean PC over assessable videos only. We also report the joint performance (JP), the percentage of all videos with SA≥\geq4 and PC≥\geq4, i.e., videos that are both faithful to the caption and physically plausible. Following VideoPhy-2 [8], we use JP as the primary metric. A high PC alone only indicates that what is shown is plausible (e.g., a nearly static video can easily appear plausible), so SA is needed to confirm that the model produces the described event.

Implementation Details. For video generation, each open-source model is run with its official checkpoint and default sampling recipe, generating one video per caption with a fixed seed of 42. HunyuanVideo-1.5 and Wan2.2-T2V-A14B are rendered at 480p, CogVideoX1.5-5B at 768p, and the remaining open-source models at 704p. Seedance 2.5 and Veo 3.1 are accessed through their official APIs at 480p and 720p, respectively. Per-model settings are listed in Suppl. Sec. B.1. For PhyRubric-Judge, we fine-tune Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct [5] on PhyRubric-Train with LoRA (rank 16) [28] on all linear layers of the language model, keeping the vision encoder and projector frozen. The judge takes the caption and 16 uniformly sampled frames, each resized to at most 448×448448\times 448. We train for 2 epochs (900 steps) with an effective batch size of 8 and a cosine learning rate schedule peaking at 10−410^{-4}. At inference, the judge decodes greedily, and we additionally compute a soft score [42, 63] as the expected rating under the probabilities of the five score tokens (Suppl. Sec. B.2). All experiments are run on NVIDIA GH200 Superchips.

4.2 Main Results

Tab. 1 reports the results of ten video generators on PhyRubric-Bench across five physics domains. We summarize the main findings below.

Physical commonsense remains far from solved. The two proprietary models lead by a wide margin: Seedance 2.5 achieves an average JP of 44.20% and Veo 3.1 36.20%, two to three times that of the strongest open-source model, HunyuanVideo-1.5-8B (14.93%). Even so, more than half of their videos are still not both faithful to the caption and physically plausible. Moreover, every open-source model has an average SA below 3, indicating that at least one primary element of the caption is typically missing from the generated video. Even among assessable videos, where the intended event does occur, their average PC never exceeds 3.5, suggesting that the event typically violates at least one expectation of major severity or above.

Video generative models handle optics best but struggle with heat and acoustics. As shown in Tab. 1, Optics is the strongest domain for eight of the ten evaluated models, and ranks second (or tied for second) for the remaining two models, Seedance 2.5 and CogVideoX1.5-5B. In contrast, Heat and Acoustics are the weakest domains for most models. Even the proprietary models reach only 30.00% (Seedance 2.5) and 15.00% (Veo 3.1) JP on Acoustics, and two open-source models score 0.00% in this domain. We conjecture that optical phenomena (e.g., reflection and shadows) are visually salient and well represented in training data, whereas thermal processes involve gradual state changes and acoustic phenomena must be conveyed through indirect visual cues (e.g., sound-induced ripples on a liquid surface), both of which are harder to render.

Semantic adherence is the main bottleneck, and physical errors are all-or-nothing. Fig. 5(a) shows the distribution of SA and PC scores. SA concentrates at 2 (50.8% of all videos), the score given when two or more primary elements of the caption are missing, while only 5.0% of videos receive a 4, the score for a video that misses only secondary details: most generated videos fail to depict the captioned event itself, before physics even comes into play. In contrast, once the event is fully shown, its physics is usually correct: as shown in Fig. 5(b), only 5.9% of videos show the event fully but violate physics (SA≥\geq4, PC<<4), compared with 16.9% that pass, meaning that 74.1% of fully shown events are rendered with plausible physics. Physical errors themselves are all-or-nothing: PC over assessable videos is bimodal, with 52.9% scoring 5, i.e., no violation at all, and 40.8% scoring 1 or 2, i.e., a fatal or core violation, whereas scores of 3 and 4, i.e., only major or minor violations, together account for 6.3%. This suggests that when current models do show the event, they either render its physics correctly or break it at the most basic level, and rarely get the core event right but slip on peripheral details.

Models take a shortcut to high PC by not showing the event. Prior protocols rate PC on every video, so a video that never attempts the event leaves nothing for physics to contradict and receives a high PC. In PhyRubric, the PC items on the central event of such a video are judged not shown, so the video is marked unassessable and excluded from PC. We define the avoidance rate of a model as the share of its videos that never show the event. Such avoidance is common: 25.0% of all videos never show the event (Fig. 5(b)), and the avoidance rate ranges from 20.0% to 44.5% across open-source models, compared with 5.7% and 8.6% for Seedance 2.5 and Veo 3.1 (Fig. 5(c)). We regard avoidance as a failure of physical commonsense rather than merely of instruction following: every caption in PhyRubric-Bench states the outcome explicitly, so a model that still renders a static scene or a different event suggests that it does not know how the stated cause produces the stated effect. If avoided videos are scored as in prior protocols, the PC score of every open-source model rises by 0.16–0.59, and the gain grows with its avoidance rate (Fig. 5(c)). LTX-Video-2B, with the highest avoidance rate (44.5%), would then rank above Cosmos-Predict2.5-14B and Wan2.2-T2V-A14B. PC alone is most misleading for Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B: under prior protocols its PC would be second only to Seedance 2.5 and above Veo 3.1, yet its JP (6.69%) ranks eighth of ten, as it rarely depicts the event.

4.3 Evaluation of PhyRubric-Judge

We assess PhyRubric-Judge by its agreement with the human labels of PhyRubric-Bench. We apply each judge to every video in PhyRubric-Bench and report two metrics on its soft score: Pearson correlation (rr) [50] with the human scores, and ROC-AUC [24] for distinguishing videos that humans rate as pass (score≥\geq4) from those rated as fail, separately for SA and PC. Suppl. Sec. B.2 reports the results of all judges on the full set of metrics adopted by prior work.

Baselines. We compare PhyRubric-Judge with four groups of judges. (1) Zero-shot VLMs: Qwen3-VL-8B, Qwen3-VL-32B, and Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B [5]. The 8B model is also the untrained starting point of our judge. (2) General video evaluators: VideoScore [26] and VideoScore2 [25], fine-tuned to rate generated videos along general quality dimensions. (3) Physics-specific evaluators: VideoCon-Physics [7] and VideoPhy-2-AutoEval [8], each fine-tuned on human annotations of its own benchmark. (4) Proprietary VLM: Gemini 4 Argon [18], a frontier closed-source model, prompted with the same instructions as our judge. Details are in the Suppl. Sec. B.3.

PhyRubric-Judge aligns best with human judgments. As shown in Tab. 2, PhyRubric-Judge achieves the best agreement with human judgments on both SA and PC across all metrics. On SA, it reaches a correlation of 0.61, well above the best open-source baseline, Qwen3-VL-32B (0.49). PC is the harder dimension: open-source zero-shot VLMs perform close to chance (AUC 0.53–0.58), and even the strongest open-source evaluator, VideoPhy-2-AutoEval, reaches only r=0.23r=0.23, despite being fine-tuned in two stages on 62K human annotations from VideoPhy and VideoPhy-2. In contrast, PhyRubric-Judge reaches 0.32 while being trained on only 3,600 automatically labeled videos. Notably, this 8B model is on par with the proprietary Gemini 4 Argon (r=0.60r=0.60 on SA and 0.310.31 on PC), showing that rubric-grounded supervision enables a small open model to match a frontier proprietary model.

PhyRubric-Judge generalizes to unseen generators and domains. PhyRubric-Train contains videos from only four of the ten generators. To test whether the judge learns physical commonsense rather than the artifacts of these four generators, Tab. 3 (a) compares its agreement on benchmark videos from these generators (Seen) and from the other six (Unseen). On unseen generators, PhyRubric-Judge loses only 0.03 in SA and 0.06 in PC correlation, and still outperforms every baseline. To test generalization across domains, Tab. 3 (b) trains five additional judges, each with one domain removed from PhyRubric-Train, and evaluates each on its held-out domain. SA correlation drops by at most 0.04, and PC correlation by at most 0.09 (on mechanics).

4.4 Error Analysis

To better understand the limitations of current T2V models, we categorize their failed items by the three levels and ten violation types in PhyRubric, with more analysis in Suppl. Sec. D.1.

The physical commonsense of current T2V models is still limited at the most basic level. As shown in Fig. 6 (a), 41.6% of the violations belong to L1 (core object principles) and 50.7% to L2 (everyday dynamics), while only 7.6% belong to L3 (attribute experience). This indicates that current models rarely fail on fine attributes, but instead break principles that hold for any object, such as persistence over time, and the way common events unfold. Fig. 6 (b) shows that the two most frequent types, missing consequence (24.0%) and permanence & count (20.4%), together account for nearly half of all violations. A permanence & count violation occurs when an object appears from nothing, vanishes, teleports, duplicates, or merges with another during the video. For example, in Fig. 7 (a), the sauce becomes fully stirred and the spoon teleports to a new position between 1.50 s and 1.62 s, a severe violation that any viewer would notice at a glance. A missing consequence violation occurs when the trigger of an event is shown but its effect never follows, or occurs at the wrong time. In Fig. 7(b), the lights are on from the start, before the finger even reaches the button. Both videos have high visual quality, yet their obvious physical errors make them distinguishable from real videos.

5 Conclusion

We presented PhyRubric, a rubric-grounded framework for diagnostic evaluation of physical commonsense in T2V generation, which fixes a caption-specific rubric before any video is seen and derives every score from evidence-grounded item verdicts. We instantiated it as PhyRubric-Bench across five physical domains and scaled it up to PhyRubric-Train, on which we trained PhyRubric-Judge, an open-source judge that outperforms existing open-source judges, matches Gemini 4 Argon, and generalizes to unseen generators and domains. Our evaluation of T2V models reveals that physical commonsense remains far from solved, and our in-depth analysis provides actionable insights for developing future T2V models.

LLM Usage Statement

Beyond the LLMs that are described in the paper, Claude models were used to assist with code implementation and to polish the writing. All LLM-generated code was reviewed by the authors.

Supplementary Material

Appendix A Dataset and Benchmark

A.1 Comparison with Prior Benchmarks

Tab. 4 compares PhyRubric with prior benchmarks that evaluate physical commonsense in text-to-video models. Each cell is determined from the benchmark’s paper and released code and data, following the criteria below.

Domains. Prior benchmarks center on mechanics, such as collisions, falling, and fluid flow. Heat is a main category only in PhyGenBench. PhyWorldBench covers heat in two of its 50 subcategories and electricity in one, about 4% and 2% of its prompts, whereas each domain makes up about a fifth of PhyRubric’s captions. No prior benchmark covers acoustics. These under-covered domains are exactly those in which the cause (e.g., an electric current, heat, or sound) is invisible, so a model must link a visible trigger to a visible effect without seeing what connects them.

Commonsense only. We mark this column when every caption can be judged from everyday experience. PhyWorldBench includes an Anti-Physics category whose prompts deliberately violate physics, PhyGenBench organizes its prompts by 27 physical laws, and T2VPhysBench builds its prompts from first-principles laws such as energy conservation. Judging these videos requires treating physical violations as correct or applying formal physics knowledge, neither of which reflects how non-experts judge videos.

Rubric. Several benchmarks pair each prompt with questions or standards: PhyGenBench generates physics questions with GPT-4o, PhyWorldBench lists physics standards per prompt, and PhysVidBench derives yes/no questions from each prompt. None of them, however, assigns a severity to its items or specifies the visible signs that count as a violation, so a failed question weighs the same whether an object vanishes or a color drifts slightly, and the score is an average of answers rather than a rule over severities. PhyRubric fixes both, and every rubric is verified by humans before any video is scored.

Train set. Only VideoPhy and VideoPhy-2 release human-labeled videos for training a judge, from which VideoCon-Physics and VideoPhy-2-AutoEval are trained. Their labels are holistic 1–5 ratings, whereas PhyRubric-Train provides item-level verdicts with timestamped evidence.

Explainable. A judge is explainable when it reports which requirement fails and what in the video supports that verdict. The judges of VideoPhy, VideoPhy-2, and PhyGenBench output scores only. PhyWorldBench and PhysVidBench are partially explainable: each yes/no answer refers to one requirement, so a negative answer indicates what is missing, but neither cites evidence from the video, and both judges answer from a text description of the video rather than from the video itself.

Open-source. We mark this column when a physics-specific judge is trained and its weights are released. VideoPhy and VideoPhy-2 release their judges, VideoCon-Physics and VideoPhy-2-AutoEval. PhyWorldBench, PhyGenBench, and PhysVidBench instead rely on general-purpose models, mainly proprietary ones (OpenAI o1, GPT-4o, and Gemini 2.5 Flash, respectively). T2VPhysBench uses human evaluation only and has no judge, which we mark as not applicable.

A.2 Statistics

Fig. 8 shows the taxonomy of PhyRubric-Bench, and Tab. 5 lists the categories of each domain and the number of training and evaluation captions. Captions average 21.1 words in PhyRubric-Train and 22.8 in PhyRubric-Bench. Each rubric contains 5.1 SA items and 7.0 PC items on average, and each PC item carries one of ten violation types (Tab. 6). The 3,788 training videos carry 45.9K item-level verdicts, and the 2,433 benchmark videos carry 29.3K.

A.3 Caption and Rubric Construction

Caption Construction. Captions are drafted one category at a time. For each of the 34 categories, Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-5.6 Sol receive the scope note of the category and the drafting instructions in Sec. E.3, and each model proposes a batch of candidates. Beyond the requirements in Sec. 3.2, the instructions add three rules. (1) A caption states the trigger and the visible outcome in plain words but never how the outcome unfolds. (2) It contains no law names, numbers, decorative adjectives, or camera directions. (3) Its outcome must hold under every reasonable rendering rather than depend on a threshold, such as how hard an object is pushed. Each candidate also comes with two hidden fields that neither the generator nor the VLM judge ever sees: one to three violation types that the event puts at risk, and an expectation briefly describing how the outcome should unfold. Both guide rubric drafting.

Candidates are first checked automatically for a well-formed record, a valid category, and the absence of numerals, and then reviewed manually in two stages. First, the categories are divided between two reviewers. Each reviewer marks every candidate in the assigned categories as keep, edit, or remove, provides a revised caption for each edit, and compares the captions within each category for repeated scenes, lack of variety, and events that belong to another domain. The other reviewer then cross-checks every decision and revision. Second, a third reviewer goes through all remaining captions to ensure consistent standards across categories. Disagreements are resolved by discussion. Review removed 242 candidates: 99 in heat, 48 in electricity, 48 in mechanics, 24 in acoustics, and 23 in optics.

Rubric Construction. Every caption in both splits receives a rubric by the same procedure. Claude Fable 5.1 drafts the rubric from the caption, the scope note of its category, its violation types and expectation, and approved rubrics from the same domain as examples, following the instructions in Sec. E.3. The instructions specify what each item may say: an SA item states a fact the caption requires and nothing else, and a PC item pairs a physical requirement with two to four visible signs of failure, constrains direction and order but never magnitude, and never requires an invisible cause such as heat, current, or sound to be seen.

Every draft is first run through a checking program, which flags a draft that is malformed, alters the caption, has too few or too many items, or makes some score from 1 to 5 unreachable. It also flags numeric thresholds, vague words, SA items that judge physics or are conditional, secondary SA items that overlap a PC item, and declared violation types that no PC item covers.

The 1,192 drafts are then divided evenly among three reviewers regardless of category. Each reviewer reads every assigned draft together with its flags and decides whether it passes, checking whether each item tests what the caption puts at risk and and whether every sign of failure is visible in the video. A draft that does not pass is revised with the LLM, checked by the program again, and reviewed until it passes. Finally, for cross-checking, each reviewer re-reads a random 10% of the rubrics approved by another reviewer, in a cycle, and agrees with the original decision in 93% of cases. The remaining cases, mostly wording refinements rather than incorrect items, are discussed and revised. Fig. 9 shows the full rubric of the desk-lamp caption in Fig. 3.

A.4 Annotation

Agentic annotator. Both splits are first labeled by Claude Sonnet 5.5 running as a tool-using agent. Videos are labeled by independent agent instances, each handling five videos from mixed generators. Every video is labeled in a fresh context, so the agent sees only its caption, rubric, and video, never the labels of other videos. The agent sees the video only through a frame-inspection tool with two operations. Overview returns 16 uniformly spaced frames of the whole clip, each stamped with its timestamp. Zoom returns up to 16 consecutive frames at the full frame rate within a time window chosen by the agent, optionally cropped to a region. For every video, the agent first takes an overview and writes a description of the whole clip before reading the rubric in detail. It then zooms at least once into the time window and region where the central event should occur, and zooms again whenever a decision hinges on a moment it has not yet seen at full frame rate. An item that involves a small object or a fast action is never decided from the overview alone. The full instructions are given in Sec. E.3.

The agent applies the verdict definitions of Sec. 3.1 with one additional requirement: an item passes only when the agent can point to the frames that show it, since the caption states what was requested, not what the video contains. For every item, the agent writes its verdict with one or two sentences of timestamped evidence, and for a failed PC item it also records which sign in the Fail statement was observed. The agent never outputs scores; SA and PC are computed from its verdicts by the rules in Sec. 3.1. PhyRubric-Train uses these labels as they are.

Human verification. For PhyRubric-Bench, the three reviewers who built the rubrics verify every verdict against the video. Each reviewer watches the video, reads every verdict together with its evidence, and keeps it or changes it; the agent’s original labels are stored separately so that every change can be counted. Generator names are hidden and videos are shuffled across generators, so that a reviewer cannot be biased toward or against a particular model. The three reviewers first verify 20 videos together to align their standards, and these are excluded from the statistics below. Next, 150 videos, 15 per generator, are each verified independently by two reviewers, with each pair of reviewers covering one third of them. The remaining videos are divided evenly among the three reviewers.

Overturn rate. Reviewers changed 2.8% of the SA verdicts and 5.6% of the PC verdicts. Most PC changes (61%) turn a pass into a fail, i.e., a violation the agent missed, typically a brief or small one, which matches the error patterns of Sec. 4.4. After verification, 88.1% of the videos keep both their SA and PC scores, and most of the remaining ones change by one point. On the doubly verified videos, the two reviewers agree on 95.3% of the verdicts (Cohen’s κ=\kappa={}0.87), so the corrections reflect what the video shows rather than the preference of one reviewer. Because PhyRubric-Train is labeled by the same agent under the same instructions, the overturn rate also approximately estimates the error rate of its training labels, about 3% for SA and 6% for PC verdicts.

Appendix B Experimental Setup

B.1 Generation Settings

Tab. 7 lists the settings of every generator. Each caption is passed verbatim as the prompt, with no prompt rewriting, style suffix, or negative prompt beyond a model’s own default. Clip length follows each model’s native recipe, between 5.0 and 6.0 seconds. Seedance 2.5 is run at 480p, 16:9, and 5 seconds, with audio and watermark disabled. Veo 3.1 (veo-3.1-generate-001) is run at 720p and 6 seconds, without audio.

B.2 Evaluation Metrics

Hard and soft judge scores. A generative judge emits an integer score, which we call the hard score. Following G-Eval [42] and Q-Align [63], we also extract the probabilities the model assigns to the tokens “1”–“5” at the position where it generates the score, and define the soft score as the expectation under the renormalised distribution:

ssoft=∑k=15k⋅p⁡(k)∑j=15p⁡(j),s^{\text{soft}}=\sum_{k=1}^{5}k\cdot\frac{p(k)}{\sum_{j=1}^{5}p(j)}, (2)

where p⁡(k)p(k) is the probability of token “kk”. Unlike the hard score, the soft score can rank clips that receive the same integer, which reflects the judge’s confidence and avoids the many ties that a five-valued integer score inevitably produces, so that correlation and ranking metrics can measure finer-grained agreement with humans.

VideoCon-Physics [7] and VideoScore [26] output continuous scores by construction (a Yes-probability and a regression output, respectively), so they have a soft score but no hard score. VideoPhy-2-AutoEval [8], like PhyRubric-Judge, emits integer scores. We compute its soft score with the same construction, without changing its prompt or decoding, so that all judges are compared on soft scores.

Metrics used by prior judges. Existing judges are validated with different metrics [7, 8, 26, 25]. We report all of them for every judge (Tab. 8) and group them into three families below, where, for each clip ii and each dimension (SA or PC), xix_{i} is the judge’s (hard or soft) score, yi∈{1,…,5}y_{i}\in\{1,\dots,5\} the human label, and nn the number of clips.

A. Correlation. These metrics measure whether the judge orders clips in the same way as humans, regardless of the score scale. We report them on both the hard and the soft score, because the prior judges validate with different score types: VideoPhy-2-AutoEval reports Pearson on its integer score, VideoScore2 on a probability-derived float.

  • •

    Pearson rr is the linear correlation between xx and yy:

    r=∑i(xi−x¯)​(yi−y¯)∑i(xi−x¯)2​∑i(yi−y¯)2.r=\frac{\sum_{i}(x_{i}-\bar{x})(y_{i}-\bar{y})}{\sqrt{\sum_{i}(x_{i}-\bar{x})^{2}}\sqrt{\sum_{i}(y_{i}-\bar{y})^{2}}}. (3)

    It ranges in [−1,1][-1,1], and a higher value indicates stronger linear agreement with human labels.

  • •

    Spearman ρ\rho is the Pearson correlation computed on ranks instead of raw scores, where clips with equal scores share the average of their ranks. It ranges in [−1,1][-1,1], and a higher value indicates that the judge ranks clips more consistently with human labels, even if the two scores are not linearly related.

B. Ranking.

  • •

    ROC-AUC splits clips by the human label into positives 𝒫={i:yi≥4}\mathcal{P}=\{i:y_{i}\geq 4\} and negatives 𝒩\mathcal{N}, and measures the probability that a positive clip receives a higher judge score than a negative one, counting ties as one half:

    AUC=1|𝒫|​|𝒩|​∑i∈𝒫∑j∈𝒩[𝟙​(xi>xj)+12​𝟙​(xi=xj)].\mathrm{AUC}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}||\mathcal{N}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{P}}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}}\big[\mathbbm{1}(x_{i}>x_{j})+\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbbm{1}(x_{i}=x_{j})\big]. (4)

    It ranges in [0,1][0,1], where 0.50.5 corresponds to random ordering and a higher value is better. It thresholds only the human label, so it applies to judge scores on any scale. Following VideoCon-Physics [7], which computes ROC-AUC on its continuous Yes-probability, we compute it on continuous scores: for judges that output integers, we use their soft scores (Eq. 2).

C. Agreement. These metrics check whether the judge’s decisions or scores match the human labels, in two ways.

(1) Binary agreement. Both scores are thresholded into pass/fail decisions, zi=𝟙​(yi≥4)z_{i}=\mathbbm{1}(y_{i}\geq 4) and z^i=𝟙​(xi≥θ)\hat{z}_{i}=\mathbbm{1}(x_{i}\geq\theta), where θ\theta is the judge’s own pass line (Tab. 9). We compute the metrics for SA and PC separately, and for their joint decision, under which a clip passes only if both pass.

  • •

    Binary accuracy is the fraction of clips with z^i=zi\hat{z}_{i}=z_{i}.

  • •

    F1 is the harmonic mean of precision (the fraction of judge-passed clips that humans also pass) and recall (the fraction of human-passed clips that the judge also passes), with pass as the positive class.

(2) Score-level agreement. Exact and within-1 accuracy are reported for judges that output integer 1–5 scores, and are computed on the hard score. They measure whether the score can be used directly on the human scale, rather than how well it ranks clips.

  • •

    Exact accuracy is the fraction of clips with xi=yix_{i}=y_{i}.

  • •

    Within-1 accuracy is the fraction of clips with |xi−yi|≤1|x_{i}-y_{i}|\leq 1, tolerating the one-point disagreements that are common among human annotators.

Both range in [0,1][0,1], and a higher value is better.

B.3 Baseline Setup

Tab. 9 lists the dimensions, native output and pass line of every judge. All baselines are run on the PhyRubric-Bench videos with their official checkpoints, prompts, frame sampling and decoding. Each baseline receives the caption and the video, but not the rubric.

VideoCon-Physics [7] and VideoPhy-2-AutoEval [8] share the mPLUG-Owl-video 7B architecture. We follow their official implementations, including the prompts (Sec. E.1) and 32 uniformly sampled frames at 224×224224\times 224. Each is queried once for SA and once for PC. VideoCon-Physics uses the normalized probability of answering “Yes” as its soft score:

s=p⁡(Yes)p⁡(Yes)+p⁡(No).s=\frac{p(\text{Yes})}{p(\text{Yes})+p(\text{No})}. (5)

VideoPhy-2-AutoEval takes its greedily decoded digit as the hard score, and its soft score follows Eq. 2.

VideoScore [26] follows its official implementation, with up to 48 uniformly sampled frames and a single prompt containing the caption (Sec. E.1). Instead of generating text, it outputs five scores in [1,4][1,4] from a regression head, one per evaluation dimension. We use text-to-video alignment as SA and factual consistency as PC.

VideoScore2 [25] follows its official implementation, with video sampled at 2 fps, its three-dimension prompt containing the caption (Sec. E.1), and sampling at temperature 0.7 with a fixed seed per clip. It first generates a reasoning trace and then an integer score for each dimension, which we parse as the hard score. Its soft score applies Eq. 2 at each score token. We use text-to-video alignment as SA and physical and common-sense consistency as PC.

Zero-shot VLMs. Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct and Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B-Instruct receive the same system prompt and input as PhyRubric-Judge (Sec. E.2), namely the SA and PC rating scales described in words, the caption, and 16 uniformly sampled frames at up to 448×448448\times 448. They decode greedily and are parsed identically. The 8B model is the base of PhyRubric-Judge.

Proprietary VLM. Gemini 4 Argon receives the same system prompt and output format as PhyRubric-Judge (Sec. E.2). The video is sent directly and sampled by the model at 3 fps, which yields about 15 frames for a five-second clip, close to the 16 frames given to the local judges. Thinking cannot be disabled, so we set it to the lowest level the model allows (LOW), and we decode at temperature 0. The integer the model outputs is its hard score. The model exposes no token probabilities, so Eq. 2 cannot be applied. Instead, in a second run, we add two fields to the requested JSON that ask the model for its probability of each score from 1 to 5, separately for SA and PC, and take the expectation of this stated distribution as the soft score.

Appendix C Additional Experimental Results

C.1 Comparison with Existing VLM Judges

Tab. 10–12 report families A–C for every judge of Tab. 2. Judges whose dimensions differ from ours are mapped to SA and PC as listed in Tab. 9. All baselines use their official checkpoints, prompts, frame sampling and decoding; implementation details are given in Sec. B. PhyRubric-Judge achieves the best result on every metric among open-source judges, and is on par with the proprietary Gemini 4 Argon.

Comparison with Gemini 4 Argon. In Tab. 10, Gemini 4 Argon leads on the hard-score rows. This is because its thinking cannot be disabled (Sec. B.3), so its integer score follows a reasoning trace, whereas the hard score of PhyRubric-Judge, like that of every other baseline, is a single greedy token without reasoning. A direct comparison of hard scores therefore favors Gemini 4 Argon. Moreover, a paired bootstrap over clips (2,000 resamples) shows that none of these gaps is significant, as all 95% confidence intervals include zero.

In Tab. 12, Gemini 4 Argon is best on binary accuracy, on SA and jointly. These numbers are inflated because it rarely predicts pass: it passes only 10% of clips on SA and 3% jointly, whereas humans pass 20% and 14%. Since most clips fail, even a trivial judge that fails every clip reaches an accuracy of 0.80 on SA and 0.86 jointly. F1 does not reward this behaviour, and PhyRubric-Judge achieves the higher F1 in every column. Moreover, its joint pass rate (17%) is close to the human rate (14%), so it yields usable per-generator scores for a leaderboard, whereas Gemini 4 Argon would leave most generators with a JP near zero (Tab. 13).

C.2 Reproducing the Leaderboard with PhyRubric-Judge

The clip-level agreement of Sec. C.1 is a demanding test. In practice, a judge is used to score a generator, where per-clip errors average out. We therefore recompute the leaderboard of Tab. 1 from judge scores (Tab. 13).

PhyRubric-Judge reproduces the human leaderboard closely (r=0.93r=0.93, ρ=0.87\rho=0.87) and keeps its JP values on the human scale, with an MAE of 4.65 points. It separates the two proprietary generators from the open-source ones by a wide margin, although it swaps their order, and it overestimates the weakest open-source generators. Gemini 4 Argon reaches a slightly higher Pearson correlation (r=0.94r=0.94), but this is driven by the two proprietary generators alone: it compresses the other eight to a JP below 3%, so it ranks them less reliably (ρ=0.81\rho=0.81) and deviates far more from the human values (MAE 12.65). PhyRubric-Judge thus provides a leaderboard that is usable in absolute terms, not only in ranking.

C.3 Ablations of PhyRubric-Judge

Tab. 14 examines four design choices of PhyRubric-Judge. Each variant trains Qwen3-VL-8B with the recipe of Sec. 4.1 and changes only one factor. Fig. 10 shows the input and output of each variant.

Should the judge see the rubric?

The annotator needs the rubric, whereas the judge takes only the caption (Sec. 3.3). We test this choice in three ways. (1) Giving the judge the rubric as input and training it to output the scores only improves correlation by 0.06 on SA and 0.05 on PC. The rubric thus carries information that the judge cannot fully recover from the caption, but every new caption would then need a rubric before the judge can be applied. (2) Giving the rubric and training the judge to output item-wise verdicts instead of scores does not help, as the scores derived from its verdicts are less accurate than directly predicted ones. (3) The rubric is of no use to the untrained model. Given the rubric, zero-shot Qwen3-VL-8B becomes worse on both dimensions, and its PC correlation falls below zero. We therefore keep the caption-only input, so that the judge applies to any new caption, and use the rubric at annotation time only.

Where should the diagnosis go?

The judge emits the scores first and the diagnosis after them. We compare two alternatives in which the diagnosis is generated first. (1) The diagnosis is the first field of the same JSON object. (2) The diagnosis is a chain of thought inside <think> tags, followed by a JSON object that holds the scores only. The diagnosis text is identical in all three cases, and only its position changes. Both alternatives lose 0.06–0.07 on SA and 0.12 on PC. The reason is that the soft score is the expectation over the score tokens (Eq. 2). When the score comes first, this distribution still reflects the uncertainty of the judge. After a committed diagnosis, it becomes nearly one-hot, and this uncertainty is lost. Scores first thus keeps an informative soft score and a diagnosis.

Does reinforcement learning help?

Starting from the SFT judge, we continue training the same LoRA with GRPO for one epoch, with 4 samples per prompt at temperature 1, a batch of 8 prompts, a learning rate of 10−510^{-5}, and no KL term. The reward is a weighted sum of four terms,

R=rSA+rPC+0.5​rfmt+0.5​rassess,R=r_{\text{SA}}+r_{\text{PC}}+0.5\,r_{\text{fmt}}+0.5\,r_{\text{assess}}, (6)

where rfmtr_{\text{fmt}} rewards a valid output format and rassessr_{\text{assess}} rewards a correct pc_assessable flag. The score terms measure how close the predicted score s^d\hat{s}_{d} is to the label sds_{d}:

rd=1−|s^d−sd|4,d∈{SA,PC}.r_{d}=1-\frac{|\hat{s}_{d}-s_{d}|}{4},\quad d\in\{\text{SA},\text{PC}\}. (7)

We run this recipe twice, (1) without thinking, starting from Default, and (2) with thinking, starting from Diagnosis as thinking, and compare each run with its own starting point.

As shown in Tab. 14(c), neither run improves over its SFT starting point, and the thinking-free run is clearly better than the one with thinking, especially on PC (rr of 0.314 vs. 0.086). A possible reason is that GRPO has mainly proven effective on reasoning tasks with verifiable answers, such as mathematics, and may bring less to a perceptual task such as judging physical commonsense in video. We leave this to future work and keep SFT as the default.

How much training data is needed?

PhyRubric-Train is split into 3,600 videos for training and 188 videos from 47 held-out captions for monitoring the training loss. All judges in this paper are trained on the 3,600-video split. We train on random 25% and 50% subsets of it (900 and 1,800 videos) with the same number of epochs (Fig. 11). SA improves only slightly with data (0.58, 0.59, 0.61), whereas PC improves steadily (0.22, 0.25, 0.32). Physical plausibility is thus the dimension that benefits most from more supervision. Since the training labels are produced automatically by the annotator, the judge can be strengthened further at low cost, by generating and labeling more videos without human annotation.

C.4 Can Prompting Fix Physical Violations?

Setup. We ask whether feeding the diagnosis back into the prompt helps a generator fix its failures. From the 245 Wan2.2-T2V-A14B videos of PhyRubric-Bench, we take the 193 that PhyRubric-Judge scores SA≤\leq3 or PC≤\leq3 and sample 100 of them, stratified by domain. Each caption is re-rendered once under two conditions with the same sampler settings: the original caption with a new seed, which controls for resampling, and a prompt of 45–70 words written by Claude Sonnet 5.5 from the caption and the judge’s diagnosis of the original video, which names the agent, states the cause before its effect, and fixes the order of events. All 200 new videos are labeled blind by the annotator with the original rubrics (Sec. A.4), and Tab. 15 compares them with the original videos.

The rewrite fixes adherence, not physics. The diagnosis-driven rewrite raises the mean SA from 2.55 to 3.19 and the SA pass rate from 11% to 31%, against 2.76 and 18% for resampling alone, and its gain over the new seed is significant. PC, in contrast, does not move: neither condition differs from the original in mean PC or in PC pass rate, and the joint pass rate rises only because more videos now pass SA. The rewrite can make the generator depict the caption, but it does not make it obey physics.

What the diagnosis changes. Fig. 12 shows an example. The diagnosis states that the balloon floats on a string and that no throw, no arc and therefore no order of events is seen. The rewrite is specific about exactly these points: it starts from the arm swinging and releasing the balloon, names the high arc above the fence and the splash, and keeps the scene of the original video. The generator follows this prompt, and SA rises from 2 to 5. The diagnosis turns the caption into a prompt that states what the generator left out.

Appendix D More Analysis

D.1 Error Analysis

The ten violation types are defined in Tab. 6 (Sec. A.2). Tab. 16 reports, for each domain, the share of assessable videos with at least one failed PC item of each type, and Tab. 17 breaks the same rates down by generator.

Adherence decays along the causal episode. Every caption in PhyRubric describes a complete episode, namely a scene, a trigger, its effect, and their order, and the SA items follow this structure. Fig. 13(a) plots the pass rate of each stage. Models render the scene most reliably, but the pass rate falls for the trigger and its effect, and falls further for their order. The decay is steepest for the weakest models. Fig. 13(b) focuses on the step from trigger to effect. In mechanics and optics, where the effect follows directly from contact or light, 68% and 70% of triggered videos show it. In heat, electricity, and acoustics, where the cause reaches the effect through an invisible medium, only 43–49% do.

Violation types follow the physics of each domain. Tab. 16 shows that the violation types are not spread evenly over the domains but follow what each domain asks for. Missing consequence is the most frequent type overall (17.3% of assessable videos) and peaks in acoustics (44.4%) and electricity (24.6%), where an invisible sound or current must produce a visible effect, against 9.1% in mechanics. Acoustics also leads in causeless motion (21.8%), since a vibration that should follow a sound is often rendered as an object that shivers on its own. Process direction concentrates in heat and electricity (11.2% and 13.0%), where a melting process reverses or a lamp switches back off. Optics carries the appearance types, namely shape and identity (11.7%), where a reflection or a refracted object does not match its source, and attribute drift (9.3%), where the color of an untouched object changes. Mechanics, where several objects interact, leads in permanence and count (18.5%), material response (8.6%), and trajectory and momentum (8.2%). Each domain thus exposes a different class of failure, and a benchmark concentrated on mechanics would leave most of these failures unmeasured.

Object permanence separates the generators, while missing consequence is shared. Tab. 17 breaks the same rates down by generator, and the two most frequent types behave differently. Permanence and count failures vary by a factor of six. Objects appear, vanish, or duplicate in 33.3% of the assessable videos of CogVideoX1.5-5B and in 22–23% of those of LTX-Video-2B and Wan2.2-TI2V-5B, but in only 5.2% for Seedance 2.5 and 8.6% for HunyuanVideo-1.5 and Cosmos-Predict2.5-14B, with Veo 3.1 in between at 12.9%. Missing consequence, in contrast, stays between 11% and 22% for every generator, and causeless motion between 6% and 13%. Missing consequence is the most frequent type for all generators except the two weakest, where permanence and count leads. Keeping objects consistent over time thus separates the generators, whereas linking a cause to its visible effect is a weakness they all share and remains the dominant failure even of the generators that largely keep objects consistent.

D.2 Qualitative Examples

Generated videos. Figs. 14–18 show one caption per domain rendered by all ten generators. The two proprietary models render the event in every example, while open-source models most often fail before physics comes into play. Avoidance rarely looks like a frozen scene. Instead, the generator skips the action the caption describes: it either shows the outcome from the first frame, as in the fish already hanging from the rod (Cosmos-Predict2.5-14B, Fig. 17) or the phone resting on the pool edge throughout (CogVideoX1.5-5B, Fig. 14), or replaces the action with a related one, such as leafing through sheet music (LTX-2.3-22B, Fig. 18). When the event is shown, the physical errors are brief and local, such as the sheet of paper that emerges from beneath the speaker (Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B, Fig. 18): a single rubric item catches it, and the verdict carries the item’s severity rather than a holistic impression.

Judge diagnoses. Fig. 19 shows the output of PhyRubric-Judge on four videos from PhyRubric-Bench. The diagnosis follows the structure of the training targets: a timestamped description of what the video shows, the caption facts that are missing, and each physical violation with the moment it occurs. When the event passes (a), the description is a complete timeline of the event. When the event never occurs (b), the judge says so and marks PC as not assessable. When physics breaks (c, d), the judge names the violation and when it occurs, such as fish that tumble with nothing touching them or balls that appear and vanish on the table.

Appendix E Prompts

This section lists the prompts used by every judge, and the instructions used to draft captions and rubrics (Sec. E.3). Baseline prompts are reproduced verbatim from the official code; {caption} is replaced by the caption of the clip and <|video|> (or the equivalent placeholder) by the video tokens.

E.1 Baseline Judges

VideoCon-Physics [7] is queried twice per clip, once for SA and once for PC, and scored as p⁡(Yes)/(p⁡(Yes)+p⁡(No))p(\text{Yes})/(p(\text{Yes})+p(\text{No})) at the answer position.

VideoPhy-2-AutoEval [8] is queried twice per clip; the first digit of the greedy output is the score.

VideoScore [26] uses one prompt for all five dimensions; the five scores are read from the regression head, and we use text-to-video alignment as SA and factual consistency as PC.

VideoScore2 [25] uses one prompt for its three dimensions and answers after a reasoning trace; we use text-to-video alignment as SA and physical/common-sense consistency as PC.

E.2 PhyRubric-Judge and Zero-shot VLMs

PhyRubric-Judge and the zero-shot Qwen3-VL models receive the same system prompt and the same user turn (the frames followed by the caption). The judge is fine-tuned on this format, while the zero-shot models see it as is.

E.3 Data Construction

The following instructions were given to the LLMs that drafted the captions and the rubrics (Sec. A.3), and to the agentic annotator (Sec. A.4); for the annotator, file paths and tool invocation details are omitted. {domain}, {category}, and {category_note} are filled per category, and {caption}, {violation_types}, {expectation}, and {examples} per caption.
